# Is 1400 a Good SAT Score? 2026 Guide, Colleges, Scholarships


## TL;DR


Yes, a 1400 is an excellent SAT score. It places you in roughly the 93rd to 94th percentile of all test-takers, meaning you outperformed about 94 out of every 100 students who sat for the exam. A 1400 is competitive at most colleges in the country, unlocks significant merit scholarships, and only falls short at a handful of ultra-selective schools. Whether you should retake depends entirely on your specific college list.


> **Quick Answer: Is 1400 a Good SAT Score?**
>
>
> Yes. A 1400 is an excellent SAT score and is substantially above the average SAT score. It puts you around the top 6–7% of recent SAT test-takers, although the exact percentile depends on the College Board reference population used. A 1400 is competitive at many public universities and selective colleges, but it is below the typical range at the most selective schools. Whether you should retake depends on your target colleges, intended major, and scholarship goals.

## What a 1400 SAT Score Actually Means


### SAT Scoring Basics


The SAT runs on a 400 to 1600 scale. It has two sections: Reading and Writing (200 to 800) and Math (200 to 800). Your total score is the sum of both sections. The[digital SAT format](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/digital-sat-prep) uses adaptive modules, but the scoring scale remains the same.


### Understanding Percentiles


When we say a 1400 puts you in the 93rd to 94th percentile, that’s the “user-group percentile,” which compares your score against recent SAT takers. There’s also a “nationally representative percentile” (about 97th for a 1400), which estimates how you’d compare against all U.S. students, including those who never took the SAT.


For college admissions, user-group percentiles matter more because they compare you with the students actually applying to colleges. If you want a deeper understanding of the difference, our guide on[SAT percentiles](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-percentiles-user-vs-national-guide) breaks this down in detail.


### What “Middle 50%” Means


You’ll see this term constantly in college admissions. The middle 50% (also called the interquartile range) represents the SAT scores of the 25th to 75th percentile of admitted students at a given school. If a school’s middle 50% is 1350 to 1500, that means 25% of admits scored below 1350 and 25% scored above 1500. Falling within this range means you’re a competitive applicant on the testing front.

## Is a 1400 SAT Score Good Enough for the Ivy League?


A 1400 SAT score can be submitted to an Ivy League school, but it is generally below the typical SAT range reported by the most selective Ivy League colleges. At these schools, a 1400 is more likely to be a relative weakness than a strength when compared with the scores of enrolled or admitted students.


That does not mean a 1400 makes admission impossible. Highly selective colleges evaluate applicants using academic performance, course rigor, extracurricular achievements, essays, recommendations, context, and other factors in addition to standardized test scores.

## Colleges You Can Get Into With a 1400 SAT Score


This is the question that actually matters. A percentile tells you where your score sits nationally, but it doesn’t tell you whether that score is competitive at the specific schools on your list. Here’s how a 1400 maps to different college tiers.


### Safety Schools (1400 Is Above the 75th Percentile)


At most state flagships and large public universities, a 1400 puts you well above the typical admitted student. Think schools like Penn State, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Ohio State, Purdue, and the University of Minnesota. Your score is a strength, not a question mark.


### Match Schools (1400 Is Within the Middle 50%)

### Reach Schools (1400 Is Near or Below the 25th Percentile)


For the Ivy League and the most selective schools in the country, a 1400 falls near the bottom of admitted student ranges. Harvard’s middle 50% is 1500 to 1580. MIT sits at 1520 to 1570. Stanford lands at 1510 to 1570.


At these schools, a 1400 is below the 25th percentile of admitted students. That doesn’t make admission impossible, but it means your score isn’t doing the heavy lifting. You’d need exceptional strength in other areas of your application.


For a broader look at how scores map to different schools, check out our full guide on[SAT scores for colleges](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-scores-for-colleges-ranges-and-admissions-guide) .


### The Dartmouth Counterpoint


Here’s something almost nobody talks about. When Dartmouth reinstated its SAT requirement in February 2024, the faculty research behind the decision revealed something striking: hundreds of less-advantaged applicants with scores in the 1400 range had been withholding their scores under the test-optional policy. In other words, a 1400 was actually helping their applications at an Ivy, not hurting them. These students were leaving a competitive advantage on the table.


This is a powerful counternarrative. A 1400 may be below the median at top schools, but it can still meaningfully strengthen an application, especially for students from underrepresented backgrounds or under-resourced schools.

### What a Retake Typically Yields


Students generally see an improvement of 30 to 70 points upon retaking, though results vary. A study published in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy found that retaking substantially improved scores and increased four-year college enrollment rates.


But here’s the catch. The jump from 1400 to 1500 is one of the hardest 100-point gains to achieve. At this level, you’re no longer filling content gaps. You’re eliminating a small number of specific, high-difficulty errors. Practitioners on Reddit’s r/Sat consistently emphasize this point: studying above 1400 requires a fundamentally different approach than studying from 1200 to 1400.


### Superscoring Works in Your Favor


Roughly 85% of four-year institutions now consider superscored results. Superscoring means schools take your highest section score from across multiple test sittings. So if you score 700 RW / 700 Math on your first attempt and then 680 RW / 750 Math on your second, your superscore becomes 700 RW + 750 Math = 1450.


This means you can focus your retake prep on just one section, which is a much more efficient use of time.


## How to Improve From 1400 to 1500+


If you decide to retake, the strategy matters as much as the decision. Here’s what works at this level.


**Start with a diagnostic.** Take a[full-length practice exam](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-exams) under real timing conditions. Don’t just note your score. Catalog every single question you got wrong or guessed on. At 1400+, you’re probably missing 8 to 12 questions total across both sections. Each one needs to be understood individually.


**Shift from content learning to error pattern analysis.** Students above 1400 face a compressed range where gains come from identifying and fixing recurring mistake types. Maybe you consistently misread “which choice best supports” questions. Maybe you lose points on systems of equations under time pressure. The fix isn’t more practice. It’s the right practice, targeted at your specific weaknesses.


**Drill targeted question sets.** Use a[SAT question bank](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/question-bank) that lets you filter by domain, skill, and difficulty. If you’re missing hard algebra questions, do 50 hard algebra questions, not another full test.


**Simulate test day.** After targeted practice, take another timed full-length test to verify improvement. The gap between untimed accuracy and timed accuracy is where many 1400-scorers lose points.


For a complete study approach, our[guide to improving your SAT by 200 points](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-to-improve-sat-score-by-200-points-5-step-plan) covers the diagnostic-first methodology in depth. Even though you’re aiming for a smaller gain, the framework applies.


## The Test-Optional Landscape Has Changed


The test-optional wave that peaked after COVID has been receding at the top end. Harvard, Yale, MIT, Stanford, Dartmouth, Brown, and others have[reinstated SAT/ACT requirements](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/28/us/sat-act-test-optional-colleges.html) . This matters for anyone with a 1400 in two ways.


First, if you’re applying to these schools, submitting is no longer optional. Your 1400 will be part of the evaluation whether you like it or not.


Second, even at schools that remain test-optional, community consensus on Reddit and college admissions forums is clear: if your score is within or above a school’s middle 50%, submit it. A 1400 meets this bar at the overwhelming majority of U.S. colleges. Withholding it would mean leaving a competitive data point off the table, exactly the mistake those Dartmouth applicants were making.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is 1400 a good SAT score for Ivy League schools?


A 1400 falls below the 25th percentile at most Ivy League schools, where middle 50% ranges typically start around 1470 to 1500. However, Dartmouth’s faculty research showed that 1400-range scores actually helped less-advantaged applicants. A 1400 alone won’t carry an Ivy application, but it’s not an automatic disqualifier either, especially when the rest of your profile is strong.


### Is 1400 good enough for merit scholarships?


Yes. A 1400 unlocks substantial merit aid at many schools. The University of Alabama offers full tuition at this score regardless of residency. The University of Miami awards up to $28,000 per year. Florida residents with a 1400 exceed the Bright Futures Academic Scholars threshold for 100% tuition coverage. Many schools with automatic merit grids place 1400 in their second-highest tier.


### What is the ACT equivalent of a 1400 SAT score?


A 1400 SAT converts to approximately a 31 ACT composite according to College Board concordance tables. If you’re curious whether the ACT might suit you better, our[ACT prep resources](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/prep) can help you explore that option.


### Should I retake the SAT if I scored 1400?


It depends on your college list. If 1400 is within or above the middle 50% at your target schools, your time is better spent on other parts of your application. If you’re aiming for top-20 schools where 1500+ is the norm, retaking is worth considering. Expect to gain 30 to 70 points, but know that improvement at this level requires targeted error elimination, not just more studying.


### Is a 700 Math / 700 Reading split good, or should one section be higher?


A balanced 700/700 is perfectly fine for most applicants. The split starts to matter if you’re applying to specific programs. Engineering and STEM programs may prefer a higher Math score (say 750+), while humanities-focused programs may value stronger Reading and Writing. Check whether your target programs publish section-level data.


### Should I submit a 1400 to test-optional schools?


Almost always yes. If your 1400 falls within or above a school’s middle 50% range, submitting strengthens your application. The only scenario where you might hold it back is if the school’s admitted student range is significantly higher (like a 1500+ median) and the rest of your application is extremely strong without it.


### What percentile is a 1400 SAT score?


A 1400 places you at approximately the 93rd to 94th user-group percentile, meaning you scored higher than about 93 to 94% of recent SAT takers. On the nationally representative scale (which includes students who never took the SAT), it’s around the 97th percentile. For more on how SAT percentiles and scoring work, see our[SAT score chart guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-score-chart-percentiles-scale-benchmarks) .


### How many students score 1400 or higher on the SAT?


Approximately 120,000 students per year out of more than 2 million test-takers reach 1400 or above. That puts you in the top 7% nationally, a number that’s meaningful on a college application at nearly every school in the country.
